Get CallVault: Android app (signed APK) · website · all apps CallVault records your own Android phone calls and keeps them on this phone. You can play a recording back, find it later by number, contact name or note, and export the audio. A web library shows what you chose to back up, and nothing else. note Recording laws vary; you are responsible for getting any consent required where you are. This is general information, not legal advice.

Start here. It decides what the rest of this site is worth to you. An ordinary Android app can't read the phone network's call audio. CallVault records through the phone's microphone path instead, so your own side is the reliable part, and on many phones the other person is clear only on speaker. An optional setting turns the speaker on for calls. Results depend on the phone. If your phone maker's own recorder does better, point CallVault at that folder and it imports those files; a stereo import is split into its real channels. Every track carries the source CallVault actually found. A track is never labeled "caller" or "other party" unless that is verified. Test one real call before you rely on any of this.
documents.s: What your phone can and can't hear

documents.t: Works without a network Recording, import, playback, search, notes and export work without a network connection. Private cloud backup, off by default Turn it on and audio uploads as private files, reachable by you and by a CallVault administrator. There are no public links. A web library Shows only backed-up recordings, at callvault.aoneahsan.com. Guest use Up to 100 recordings without an account. Signing in with Google removes the count limit. Yours to remove Delete one recording from this phone or everywhere, or delete the account and its cloud files. Facts worth having early. CallVault runs on Android 8.0 and newer. It has no ads. It counts usage with analytics services, and they never receive recordings, notes, numbers or names. There is no iOS version. CallVault isn't on Google Play. It ships as a signed APK you download from the CallVault website.
New here? Start with Install CallVault. Wondering what backup costs? Read Plans and Family. Something missing from a call? Open Troubleshooting.
Administrators get an extra surface on top of the ordinary app. Everybody else never sees it, and the server refuses a privileged write from anyone else even if they find the screen.

On the web it is /admin. On the phone it is Settings → Admin panel. Administrator reach is a grant checked against the server each time you open it, so nobody arrives at it by typing a URL. Somebody without the grant gets a plain "admin access required" panel with a link back to the app, never a raw error and never somebody else's data. There is always a way back to your own recordings, because an administrator is also an ordinary user with a library of their own.

The dashboard opens on Overview: the number of accounts on the platform, how many were active in the last 14 days, and a chart of recent activity across it. Six tabs sit beside it, the same six the web rail carries: Overview, the totals above. Users: the list of accounts, each one opening its user detail. Plans, Releases, Cloud usage and the audit log: the administrator tools added in 1.3.0, all covered on Plans and releases. Roles: who holds administrator access and how it was granted, on Roles & access.

Be plain about this, because the privacy pages are: an administrator can open the private files a user has backed up. There are no public links to any of them, and no way to reach one without that grant, but the grant itself is real reach over real audio. Every privileged write lands in an append-only audit log carrying the actor, the action, the target, and the before and after values, and nothing in that log can be edited or removed. That log records changes. It is not a record of every time a file is opened. If you hold administrator access, assume your work is on the record, because it is.

documents.t: Plans and releases is where the release policy every phone reads, the plan limits the server enforces, individual grants, cloud usage and the audit log all live.

Every phone reads the release policy you set here, and every account gets the limits you set here. These screens are admin-only and reached from the admin rail. The server refuses every write from anyone else, and each write lands in the audit log.

Open Admin · Releases. Fill Publish a release from the GitHub Release and its SHA256SUMS: version name, version code, download URL, SHA-256, signing certificate SHA-256 and size in bytes. Set the channel to Prerelease (device QA) or Stable. Select Publish release row. The updater refuses any APK whose hash, version code or signer differs from that row, or whose package name differs from the installed app, so publish the row from the release files rather than from memory. A version code is unique within its channel. Rows are never deleted through the API, so retire one by disabling it, which takes it out of the policy immediately.

Release policy is what every phone is told. It carries the latest release, the minimum supported version code, the mandatory-after date, the offline grace in days (1 to 30, default 14), the check interval in hours (1 to 168, default 24), and whether the policy is enabled. A phone below the minimum enters updater-only mode. Its library stays readable and new recording pauses until the update is installed, and the phone says so on screen rather than going quiet. Lower the grace with a reason: it is what stands between someone traveling and a paused recorder.

Open Admin · Plans. Fill Create a plan: plan id, display name, price per month, price per year, cloud storage in GB, per recording in MB, objects, uploads per hour. Select Save plan. The plan id is the immutable key. The four limits on the row are what the server enforces, which is why raising one is an admin edit rather than a release.

Change a user's plan takes the account, the plan, the end date and a note that shows in provenance. Override one user's limits takes cloud storage and uploads per hour for that one account, with a reason; an empty field keeps the plan's value. Grant provenance shows where the account's current plan came from. Grants on the same plan extend and never shorten. A renewal carrying an earlier end date leaves the later one in place. Family is granted with a seat count: never below 3, and never below the members already in the household.

documents.t: Admin · Cloud usage shows the stored audio across all accounts, then a row for each account carrying the effective limit after its plan and any override. Adjust limits opens the plans page with that account already selected.

Nothing to do here. Migrate legacy audio, on the Admin · Cloud usage tab, works in batches of up to 50 across all accounts: it copies each file into private storage, verifies the checksum, deletes the public file and clears the old public link. The migration ran on 2026-09-17, and no public recording file remains.
Admin · Audit log is append-only. Every privileged write adds one row with the actor, the action, the target and the before and after values, and nothing there can be edited or removed.
CallVault keeps its access model simple and defends it in depth.

User — sees and manages only their own recordings. Admin — additionally sees the admin dashboard and can manage other users. Your role lives on your profile. You can edit your own display name, but you cannot change your own role or account status — those are locked and can only be changed by a privileged, server-side action.

CallVault's apps talk to the database with an ordinary, publicly-shippable key. What an admin can additionally see is granted by the database's row-level security rules — an admin's queries are allowed to reach every user's rows, while a normal user's queries match only their own. The check uses a live "is this caller an admin?" test on the server, not anything baked into the sign-in token, so revoking admin takes effect immediately.

Changing a role, disabling an account, or deleting another user is never done directly by the app. Those run through dedicated server-side functions that verify the caller is an admin before acting. The app never holds the elevated credentials that could bypass the rules.
A disabled account matches no data rules at all, so it sees zero rows — and the web app routes it to a clear "account disabled" screen rather than an empty app.
Open any account from the admin dashboard user list to reach its detail screen, where the account's activity and controls live.

Change role — promote a user to admin or demote back to user. Disable / re-enable — a disabled user is immediately locked out (they see no data and the web app sends them to the "account disabled" screen). Re-enabling restores access. Delete the user — removes the account, its profile, all of its recording metadata, and its backed-up audio.

Every one of these runs through a server-side function that first confirms the caller is a current administrator, then performs the change with elevated privileges the app itself never holds. The confirmation dialogs name the exact action (for example, Disable rather than a generic "confirm") so there's no ambiguity about what you're about to do. Deletion of a user is permanent — the same shape as a user deleting their own account.
CallVault keeps your recordings in two places at most, and the second one is optional.

The phone holds a local SQLite database, and it is the authoritative copy. A recording is created there, a note or a favorite is written there first, and the whole library keeps working with no network connection at all. It holds each call's details: the number, the direction, when it started, how long it ran, which SIM handled it, the audio format and the file size, plus your notes and favorites, and a small settings store for things like appearance, language and the Wi-Fi-only upload preference. A contact name is stored too when an imported recording carried one; CallVault never reads your address book. Guests never go past this point. Up to 100 recordings stay on the phone without an account, and at 100 new recording pauses while everything already there keeps playing, searching and exporting. Signing in with Google removes the count limit.

documents.t: Each recording's details are mirrored to CallVault's servers and scoped to your account. There is no audio there. It is only the facts about a call, which are sensitive on their own, so they are account-scoped exactly as the audio is.

documents.t: The audio files go to CallVault's servers as private files only you and a CallVault administrator can reach. There are no public links to any of them. CallVault checks each file against the 100 MB per-file cap before uploading, and deletes the stored file when you delete the recording everywhere. Your cloud usage is summed from what is actually stored, so the space comes back on the next read.
documents.s: The audio, once backup is on

documents.t: Keeping the audio apart from the call details lets the web library work from the cloud copy alone, while the phone keeps the authoritative offline one. See the sync pipeline for how a recording moves between them.
Read Private cloud backup for what your plan limits, or Security and privacy for who can reach what.
A recording is usable the moment the call ends. Backup happens afterwards, in the background, and every step of it is visible on one screen.

Those are the six states CallVault actually stores against a recording, and they read in order. Recorded means the file is on the phone. Pending upload means it is waiting its turn. Uploaded means the audio has reached CallVault's servers as a private file. Synced means the call's details are mirrored too, and the recording is done. None of this runs while private cloud backup is off. Uploads run on Wi-Fi by default, and a setting in the same place allows mobile data.

A call is often several tracks, and the pipeline treats each one separately. A track is pending upload, then uploading, then uploaded, then synced, and a track that has stopped for good is failed. The recording reaches Synced when every one of its tracks has, which is why a call can sit at Uploading while one track is already done.
documents.s: Each track moves on its own

documents.t: A dropped connection costs you nothing. Neither does a brief server problem. It goes back a step and is retried on an increasing delay, with separate counters for the upload leg and the details leg. A flaky connection usually resolves itself while you do nothing at all.

Some failures aren't worth retrying forever. The common one is size: CallVault checks a file against the 100 MB per-file cap before it starts uploading, so an oversize recording is never sent at all. It stays on the phone with the reason attached, and it appears under Needs attention in Backup & sync health, which is a list on that screen rather than a state on the recording. Only the cloud copy is skipped; the recording itself is where it always was. Read the reason before you retry.

CallVault never removes a recording from the phone before that recording is synced and its checksum verified. That rule holds whatever else you choose. What you choose is how long the phone keeps a copy after that, under Settings → Keep local files: Keep all recordings on this device, which never removes anything. Remove from device once synced, the default. Keep 7 days after sync. Keep 30 days after sync.
documents.s: What happens to the phone copy

documents.t: Open Settings → Storage & sync → Backup & sync health, which sits beside the Private cloud backup switch. It shows the queue, the retries, a row for each phone you use, and the Needs attention list, which is where anything that stopped waits with its reason attached.
Private cloud backup covers turning the switch on and what your plan allows.
Call recordings are among the most sensitive things a phone holds. CallVault is built around that, and the limits are on this page beside the promises.

There's no advertising SDK. Analytics counts screens and features only; see the Privacy Policy; while private cloud backup is off, which is its state until you turn it on, nothing about a call leaves the phone at all. Stay signed out and the phone keeps working exactly the same.

Recordings are written to app-private internal storage. No other app on the phone can read them, and nothing puts them in the shared media folders where a gallery or a file manager would find them. What you export to Downloads yourself is a copy you have chosen to move out. An optional app lock puts your fingerprint, your face or the device PIN in front of the app. The biometric data never leaves the phone; Android holds it and answers yes or no.

The app refuses plaintext HTTP entirely. Cleartext traffic is disabled app-wide at the platform level, so a misconfigured endpoint fails rather than falling back, and CallVault trusts only the system certificate store. A certificate a user or a proxy has installed on the phone is not trusted, which means an intercepting proxy cannot quietly sit between the app and its uploads. CallVault does not pin certificates. Trusting the system store and refusing user-installed ones is the boundary it actually enforces, and it is stated here rather than implied.

Every recording and every call detail belongs to the account that made it. Administrator reach is a separate grant on top of that, checked against the server each time the dashboard is opened rather than remembered from a previous visit. Roles & access covers how that grant is given and taken away, and every privileged write lands in an append-only audit log described on Plans and releases. Two-step sign-in adds an authenticator code after Google, and is required for administrators. Apps and assistants you connect under Other apps read only, never contact names or phone numbers, and reach audio only through a 10-minute link you allowed; CallVault for developers lists exactly what each can read.

There is no end-to-end encryption. If that is your requirement, this is the wrong tool for you, and you should read that as the hard limit it is. A CallVault administrator can reach the audio you back up. There are no public links to a recording, so nothing is one forwarded URL away from a stranger, but the grant itself is real reach over real audio, and a service that can reach your audio should say so. The web library shows only backed-up recordings. It keeps no library of its own. That is by design. Account deletion can need another pass. Profile shows processing, success or an error message. If it says "Still processing on the server", reopen Delete account to resume the saved request. For another error or one that persists, contact CallVault using the address on Deleting recordings and your account. An upload with an unclear outcome remains open for administrator review; an empty file listing does not prove its cloud copy is gone.
Private cloud backup covers what the switch turns on, and Deleting recordings and your account covers taking it all back.

CallVault is a single Flutter codebase that produces two very different products: flutter build apk produces the native Android recorder, with a Kotlin engine for call capture and the full on-device experience. flutter build web produces the web dashboard — a public landing page, the signed-in user app at /app, and the admin dashboard at /admin — as a single-page app. A conditional entry point picks the right composition root at build time, so the two builds share the same models, screens, and data code wherever it makes sense.

Anything that touches the device's file system directly can only run on the phone. If such code were reachable from the web build, the web build simply wouldn't compile. So CallVault keeps a clean boundary: The device-only capture-and-file code lives in native-only modules the web build never imports. Shared screens (profile, recording detail) are written to be web-safe; the web app plays audio by streaming from a URL, never from a local file. The private cloud backup client has a web-safe form for the browser and a separate native one for the phone, which streams uploads rather than holding a whole recording in memory. The web build is the gate: it's compiled after any change that the web side could reach, so the boundary can't drift silently. This is why the same app can be both a real recorder and a browser dashboard without shipping device internals to the web.

Anyone who can sign in to your Google account could otherwise make a key. Two-step sign-in adds a six-digit code from an authenticator app, and with it on, showing a key again always needs a fresh code.

CallVault emails you when a key is made, when an assistant connects, when two-step is turned on or off, when a recovery code is used and when a webhook address is turned off after failing. Each email names where the change came from, like "CallVault app on an Android phone", so one you didn't make stands out.

The CallVault API is a read-only REST API over HTTPS. You send an access key and get JSON back: your recordings' details, the notes on them, a 10-minute audio link, your plan and your household. There are no write or delete routes. Every address below starts with: https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/api/v1 The machine-readable description is the OpenAPI 3.1 document, also served as Markdown. Both answer without a key, and both are built from the same definition the routes are, so they can't drift apart.

Route Permission Answers with GET /recordings recordings:read A page of your recordings, newest first GET /recordings/{id} recordings:read One recording's details GET /notes/{id} notes:read The note on one recording GET /audio_link/{id} audio:read One recording's audio facts and a 10-minute download link GET /plan_and_use account:read Your plan, its limits and today's use GET /household household:read The household you belong to, if any GET /token none What the key you sent may do GET /openapi.json, GET /openapi.md none, no key This API, described {id} is always a recording's id, the id field that GET /recordings returns.
A single record arrives as { "data": { … } }. A list arrives as { "data": [ … ], "meta": { "next_cursor": …, "limit": … } }. Responses are never cached (cache-control: no-store).

An error arrives as: { "error": { "code": "scope_required", "message": "This credential needs the audio:read permission.", "details": { "scope": "audio:read" }, "correlation_id": "req_4c1f9a0b7e2d6a35" } } Status code What happened 400 invalid_request A query value is wrong, like limit=500, or the cursor expired 401 invalid_token The key is missing, mistyped, unknown, expired or turned off 403 scope_required The key wasn't given the permission this route needs 404 not_found No such record on your account, or a recording with no note or no uploaded audio 405 method_not_allowed Anything but GET 429 rate_limited Over 120 a minute for this key, or over your plan's daily requests 500 internal Our fault. Send us the correlation_id and we can find it The message is written for a person and safe to show. A record that belongs to someone else answers exactly like one that doesn't exist.

Lists return 20 at a time. Ask for up to 50 with limit. When meta.next_cursor is not null, send it back as cursor with the same filters and sort to get the next page: curl "https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/api/v1/recordings?limit=50&cursor=$NEXT" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALLVAULT_KEY" A cursor lasts 15 minutes and only works with the filters and sort it was made for. If it expires, start again without it.

Every answer carries ratelimit-limit, ratelimit-remaining and ratelimit-reset (seconds until the window resets) for the tighter of your two limits: 120 requests a minute for this key, and your plan's daily allowance across all keys and assistants, which resets at midnight UTC. A 429 also carries retry-after. Wait that many seconds before trying again: a refused request still counts, so retrying in a tight loop only keeps you refused.

curl "https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/api/v1/recordings?started_at.gte=2026-11-01T00:00:00Z&limit=2" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALLVAULT_KEY" { "data": [ { "id": "3f6b2c1e-8d4a-4e7b-9c15-2a0d7e6f4b91", "title": "Incoming call, 21 Nov, 13:49", "started_at": "2026-11-21T13:49:37+00:00", "duration_seconds": 734, "labels": ["phone_call", "starred", "Pixel 8"], "has_audio": true, "has_note": true, "created_at": "2026-11-21T14:02:05+00:00", "updated_at": "2026-11-21T14:02:11+00:00" }, { "id": "b81e04d7-52c9-4a3e-8f60-d7c2a91e5b08", "title": "Outgoing call, 20 Nov, 16:42", "started_at": "2026-11-20T16:42:03+00:00", "duration_seconds": 95, "labels": ["phone_call", "Pixel 8"], "has_audio": false, "has_note": false, "created_at": "2026-11-20T16:44:18+00:00", "updated_at": "2026-11-20T16:44:18+00:00" } ], "meta": { "next_cursor": "eyJyIjoicmVjb3JkaW5ncyIs…", "limit": 2 } } Field Meaning title Made from the direction and the start time in your own time zone. Never a contact name or number. started_at, duration_seconds When it started, and how long it is in whole seconds labels phone_call or microphone, starred when you starred it, and the phone it was recorded on has_audio Whether its audio has finished uploading to your private cloud. Only then does /audio_link have a file. has_note Whether you saved a note on it Query options: started_at.gte and started_at.lt take an ISO 8601 time; sort is -started_at (the default, newest first) or started_at. A recording you asked to delete is gone from every answer at once, before its files are removed. GET /recordings/{id} answers with one of these records.

curl https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/api/v1/notes/3f6b2c1e-8d4a-4e7b-9c15-2a0d7e6f4b91 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALLVAULT_KEY" { "data": { "id": "3f6b2c1e-8d4a-4e7b-9c15-2a0d7e6f4b91", "note": "Plumber confirmed Thursday 9 am, quote 240." } } The note is the text you typed, or kept after speaking it. A recording with no note answers 404; check has_note first to save a request.

curl https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/api/v1/audio_link/3f6b2c1e-8d4a-4e7b-9c15-2a0d7e6f4b91 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALLVAULT_KEY" { "data": { "id": "3f6b2c1e-8d4a-4e7b-9c15-2a0d7e6f4b91", "asset_kind": "original", "mime_type": "audio/mp4", "size_bytes": 5873664, "duration_seconds": 734, "uploaded_at": "2026-11-21T14:02:11+00:00", "download_url": "https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/recording-asset-download?link=cvdl_…", "expires_at": "2026-11-21T14:22:40+00:00" } } Each request makes a new link to the recording's main audio file. Download it with a plain GET; the link itself is the credential, so send no key with it: curl -o call.m4a "$DOWNLOAD_URL" The link stops working at expires_at, 10 minutes after it was made, or as soon as the key that asked for it is turned off, whichever comes first. A player may fetch it in parts with Range requests; after 20 requests the link is used up. Every link you ask for is written to your account's audit log. asset_kind says which file you get: original for a single-track recording, or the combined or channel file CallVault keeps as the main one for an imported recording. A recording whose audio hasn't finished uploading answers 404.

curl https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/api/v1/plan_and_use \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALLVAULT_KEY" A list with one record, yours: plan_id and plan_name, via (how you have the plan: grant, household, override or default), plan_ends_at, your private cloud limits and use in bytes and files, the largest file your plan accepts, and the open-platform limits (access_keys_max, api_requests_per_day, webhook_addresses_max, assistant_connections_max) beside requests_today. A null limit means the plan sets none.

curl https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/api/v1/household \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALLVAULT_KEY" { "data": [ { "id": "e4a7c2f9-3d18-4b6e-9a05-7c1f2b8d6e43", "name": "Harbour Lane", "role": "member", "seat_limit": 5, "seats_used": 4, "created_at": "2026-10-02T08:15:00+00:00" } ], "meta": { "next_cursor": null, "limit": 20 } } An empty list means you're not in a Family household. The API never says who the other members are, and never reaches their recordings.

Connect Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code or Cursor to CallVault, then ask about your recordings in plain words, like "How many calls did I record last week?" The assistant can read only what you tick on CallVault's consent page, and it can't change or delete anything. Every assistant uses the same address: https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/mcp Copy it from Other apps → Assistants in the app or the web library, which also show these steps.

In Claude, open Settings, then Connectors, and choose Add custom connector. Name it CallVault and paste the address above. Choose Connect. CallVault opens so you can sign in and pick what Claude may read.

In ChatGPT, open Settings, then Apps & Connectors, then Advanced settings, and turn on Developer mode. Choose Create, name it CallVault and paste the address above. Choose Connect, sign in to CallVault and pick what ChatGPT may read.

In a terminal, run: claude mcp add --transport http callvault https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/mcp Start Claude Code, type /mcp, pick callvault and choose Authenticate. Your browser opens CallVault so you can sign in and pick what it may read.

In Cursor, open Settings, then MCP, and choose Add new MCP server. Paste this into mcp.json: { "mcpServers": { "callvault": { "url": "https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/mcp" } } } Save, then choose Connect next to callvault. CallVault opens so you can sign in and pick what it may read.

Connecting opens CallVault's consent page in your browser. It names the assistant and the site you go back to afterwards, shows the Google account you're signed in with, and lists what the assistant may read with a tick beside each. Audio downloads is off unless you tick it, because the file is the whole call, including the other person's voice. With two-step sign-in on, Allow asks for a code from your authenticator, unless this browser is remembered. Don't allow shares nothing. If the page says CallVault doesn't know the app, allow it only if you set it up yourself. If you're already at your plan's limit of connected assistants (3 on Free, 10 on Pro, 25 on Family), it says so; disconnect one first. You get an email naming the assistant, what it may read and whether audio is allowed.

Tool What it gets Needs list_recordings Your recordings, newest first, with their details. 50 at a time, with a cursor for more. Takes started_at.gte, started_at.lt and sort. Recording details get_recordings One recording's details, by its id Recording details get_notes The note on one of your recordings Your notes get_audio_link A 10-minute download link for one of your recordings Audio downloads list_plan_and_use Your plan, its limits and today's use Plan and use list_household Your household's name, your role and seats in use Household An assistant sees only the tools you allowed; the rest don't appear in its list. Every tool is marked read only, so a careful client won't stop to ask before using one. None of them change or delete anything, so nothing ever waits for you to confirm a removal. The fields are the same as the API's. Titles look like "Incoming call, 20 Nov, 16:42": no contact name or phone number reaches an assistant, ever. Your note text is passed to the assistant as data, your own words, never as instructions to it. Each question an assistant asks uses your plan's daily requests, shared with your access keys, and each assistant may ask 120 times a minute.
documents.s: What an assistant can ask for

documents.t: Change, star, rename or delete a recording, a note or anything else. Read a recording's audio unless you ticked Audio downloads. With it ticked, it gets a link, not a transcript: CallVault doesn't send call audio to an assistant as text. See your contacts, another household member's recordings, your keys or your two-step settings. Manage keys, webhooks, two-step sign-in or other connections. Those need you, signed in to CallVault.

Connected assistants are listed under Other apps → Assistants with the day each connected and when it last asked something. Rename changes the name shown in your list. Disconnect ends it at once: its next question is refused, and any audio link it asked for stops working. To connect it again, go through the consent page again.

Transport: Streamable HTTP, stateless, one endpoint. JSON-RPC batches are refused. Discovery: an unauthenticated request gets 401 with WWW-Authenticate pointing at the protected-resource metadata, https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/mcp/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource. Authorization: OAuth 2.1 with PKCE (S256) and dynamic client registration, through CallVault's Supabase Auth server, https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/auth/v1. The person picks permissions on CallVault's own consent page; CallVault checks its own record of that choice on every call, so a disconnect ends a live token at once rather than when it expires. Origins: browser requests are accepted from claude.ai, chatgpt.com and openai.com and their subdomains, and from localhost. A request with no Origin header, like a desktop client's, is accepted. Access keys: an access key sent as a Bearer token also works here, for a script that wants MCP rather than REST.
documents.s: For people building an MCP client

documents.t: An access key lets your own script or tool read your CallVault account through the API. Every key is read only. You make it under Other apps → Access keys, tick what it may read, and send it in the Authorization header of each request.

Open Other apps → Access keys in the app or the web library. Choose Make an access key. Give it a name that tells you where it's used, like "Backup script on the NAS". Under What it may read, tick at least one thing. The permissions are listed on the overview. Under Stops working, pick Never, In 30 days, In 90 days or In a year. Every key is read only, so any of these is allowed. A shorter life is safer. Choose Make key, then copy it. The key is shown in full once, right there. CallVault keeps only a hash to recognise it and a sealed copy for showing it again, and emails you that a key was made. A key is cv_pat_, 43 random characters, an underscore and an eight-character checksum: cv_pat_7Hq2…_3a9f0c1e cv_pat_ and the next four characters are what your list shows, so you can tell keys apart without revealing one. The checksum means a mistyped key is refused before CallVault looks it up.

Put the key in the Authorization header as a Bearer token: curl https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/api/v1/recordings \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALLVAULT_KEY" Keep it on a machine you control, in an environment variable or a secrets store, never in a web page or a shared repository. Anyone holding it reads what you ticked until it stops or you turn it off.

GET /v1/token answers with the key's own facts and counts as one request: curl https://bnlxrjjwawyampjbfqnu.supabase.co/functions/v1/api/v1/token \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $CALLVAULT_KEY" { "data": { "kind": "pat", "user_id": "9c2d5e7a-1b3f-4c8d-a6e2-0f4b7d9c1a35", "client_id": null, "scopes": ["notes:read", "recordings:read"] } }
documents.s: Checking what a key can do

documents.t: You can show a key again with Show again, but only within 10 minutes of signing in. Signed in longer ago than that, CallVault asks you to sign in once more and brings you straight back to the key. With two-step sign-in on, that fresh sign-in must include a code from your authenticator. Two things never show a key, on purpose: A remembered phone or browser. It skips the code for ordinary sign-ins, not for showing a secret. A recovery code. It gets you into your account so you can set up a new phone. It does not show keys or webhook secrets. The rule is there because a session someone else picked up on a shared computer should not be enough to read every key you own.
documents.s: Showing a key again: the 10-minute rule

documents.t: Replace makes a new key with the same name and permissions. The old one keeps working for 24 hours, so you can swap the new one into your script without a gap, and then stops. A key that never stops gets a replacement that never stops; a key with an end date gets a replacement that stops in 90 days.
Turn off ends a key at once. The next request with it is refused with invalid_token, and any audio link it asked for stops working too.

Your plan sets how many keys you can have at once: 5 on Free, 25 on Pro, 50 on Family. At the limit, Make an access key tells you so; turn one off to make another. Requests from every key share your plan's daily allowance, described on the overview.
Changes to what outside apps can do with CallVault, newest first. The app's own releases are in the main changelog.

The first release. API v1, read only: recordings, notes, audio links, plan and use, household, with cursor pages, the OpenAPI 3.1 document and read-only access keys that stop Never, in 30 days, 90 days or a year. MCP server for Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code and Cursor, with six read-only tools and a consent page where audio is off unless ticked. Webhooks: recording.created and recording.upload_finished, signed the Standard Webhooks way, with eight tries over about 28 hours. Two-step sign-in on the phone and in the web library, with ten recovery codes and an optional seven-day remembered phone or browser. How it works. Security and Other apps in the web library as well as the Android app.

With two-step sign-in on, signing in to CallVault asks for a six-digit code from an authenticator app as well as your Google account. Someone who gets into your Google account still can't open your recordings. It's optional for everyone, and required for CallVault's own team. It lives under Security: on the phone at Settings → Privacy & security → Security, and in the web library in the side rail, or the Security row on the Profile tab on a narrow screen. Both show the same settings.

Open Security and choose Set up two-step sign-in. Add CallVault to your authenticator. Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, 1Password or any app that shows six-digit codes works. On the phone, Open in authenticator app adds it directly, or scan the QR code from another device. In the web library, scan the QR code with your phone. If the camera won't read it, type the key shown below it into the app instead. Type the six-digit code it shows, and choose Turn on two-step. Codes change every 30 seconds; type the one showing now. Save your ten recovery codes: copy all ten, or download them as callvault-recovery-codes.txt. They're shown now and never again, so keep them somewhere away from this phone. Tick I've put these codes somewhere safe, then Finish. Two-step is on once the codes are made, and CallVault emails you that it was turned on.
After you sign in with Google, CallVault asks for the six-digit code from your authenticator, on the phone and in the browser alike. Type it and choose Continue.

Under the code there is a box: Remember this phone for 7 days in the app, Remember this browser for 7 days in the web library. It's unticked every time. Leave it unticked on a shared device. Ticked, that phone or browser skips the code on sign-in for seven days from that moment. Signing in again doesn't extend it; after seven days it asks once more. Three things still ask for a code on a remembered device: showing an access key or a webhook secret again; admin pages; turning two-step off or making new recovery codes. A remembered browser can Allow an assistant on the consent page without a code, because an assistant can only read. Security → Remembered phones and browsers lists each one with the day it stops being remembered. Forget ends one; Forget all ends every one. Signing out on a remembered phone or browser forgets it too.
documents.s: Remembering a phone or browser for seven days

documents.t: Each of the ten codes signs you in once in place of the six-digit code: choose Use a recovery code instead, then type it, with or without the dash. Security shows how many are left and warns you when you're running low. Make new recovery codes replaces the whole set; it asks for a code from your authenticator and a sign-in within the last 10 minutes, and the old codes stop working as soon as the new ones appear. Using one emails you, so a code you didn't use stands out.

Sign in with Google, choose Use a recovery code instead, and type one of your codes. Two-step stays on. Straight away, open Security and choose Moved to a new phone. You have 10 minutes after the recovery code to start it. Add CallVault to the authenticator on your new phone and type its code. The old phone's codes stop working once the new one is confirmed. A recovery-code sign-in lasts 12 hours and does less than a normal one: it can't show keys or webhook secrets and can't open admin pages. Setting up the new phone gives you a full sign-in again.

Write to aoneahsan@gmail.com from the address on your CallVault account. After we've checked it's really you, a CallVault admin resets your two-step sign-in: it turns two-step off, deletes your recovery codes and forgets your remembered phones and browsers. You get an email when it's done, and you can set it up again with your new phone. An admin's own two-step is never reset this way; only the owner can reset it, on the server.
documents.s: If you lose your phone and your recovery codes

documents.t: Turn off two-step asks for a code from your authenticator, and you must have signed in within the last 10 minutes. After it, signing in needs only your Google account, your recovery codes are deleted and remembered phones and browsers are forgotten. CallVault emails you about the change. Team accounts can't turn it off: admin pages stay locked until two-step is on.
Security → Recent sign-ins lists where your account signed in and how: Google, Google and a code, or Google and a recovery code. Sign out everywhere else ends every other session and keeps this one.

A webhook tells your own server the moment something happens in CallVault: a recording is added to your account, or its audio finishes uploading. CallVault sends a signed POST with the recording's details, never a contact name, a phone number, note text or audio. Fetch those with an access key when you need them. Messages are signed the Standard Webhooks way, so any library that implements it can check them.

Open Other apps → Webhooks in the app or the web library and choose Add an address. Paste an https:// address. CallVault doesn't send to plain http. Under Send when, tick one or both events. Choose Add address, then copy the Signing secret that appears. It starts with whsec_. CallVault checks the address before saving it, and again before every send. It refuses: anything but https, and ports other than 443 and 8443; a username or password inside the address (check the signing secret on your server instead); an address longer than 2,048 characters; a name that points to a private, local or loopback network; CallVault's own servers. Your plan sets how many addresses you can have: 3 on Free, 20 on Pro, 40 on Family. The signing secret follows the 10-minute rule: you can show it again only within 10 minutes of signing in, with a code when two-step is on.

POST /hooks/callvault HTTP/1.1 content-type: application/json user-agent: CallVault-Webhooks/1.0 webhook-id: msg_6f1c0e9a4b2d4c7e8a5f3b1d9e0c2a74 webhook-timestamp: 1795269731 webhook-signature: v1,KXfyLaCC7f32HlkcICIKQdzHqNy5ZrCVV+Yuevpl9DY= {"type":"recording.created","timestamp":"2026-11-21T14:02:11.204Z","data":{…}} Part Meaning webhook-id The event's id. It stays the same on every retry and on Send again, so use it to ignore a repeat. webhook-timestamp When this attempt was signed, in Unix seconds webhook-signature One or more v1,<signature> values separated by spaces type The event, from the list below timestamp When the event happened data The event's details

A recording reached your CallVault account: synced from the phone or imported. data has the same fields, under the same names, as a recording in the API, minus has_audio and has_note. { "type": "recording.created", "timestamp": "2026-11-21T14:02:11.204Z", "data": { "id": "3f6b2c1e-8d4a-4e7b-9c15-2a0d7e6f4b91", "title": "Incoming call, 21 Nov, 13:49", "started_at": "2026-11-21T13:49:37+00:00", "duration_seconds": 734, "labels": ["phone_call", "starred", "Pixel 8"] } }

A recording's main audio file finished uploading to your private cloud. From now on GET /audio_link/{id} has a file to link to. id is the recording's id. { "type": "recording.upload_finished", "timestamp": "2026-11-21T14:06:48.517Z", "data": { "id": "3f6b2c1e-8d4a-4e7b-9c15-2a0d7e6f4b91", "asset_kind": "original", "duration_seconds": 734, "size_bytes": 5873664, "uploaded_at": "2026-11-21T14:06:47+00:00" } } The two events for one recording can arrive in either order: on a slow connection the audio may finish before the recording's details reach the server. Don't rely on recording.created coming first.

Sent only when you choose Send a test on an address, to that address alone. { "type": "webhook.test", "timestamp": "2026-11-21T14:10:02.031Z", "data": { "message": "Test event" } } Nothing is sent for a person whose account is being deleted, and a change that fails to save sends nothing: an event is written in the same database step as the change itself.

The signature is a base64 HMAC-SHA256 over {webhook-id}.{webhook-timestamp}.{raw body}, keyed with the base64-decoded part of your secret after whsec_. Check it on the raw bytes you received; parsing the JSON and serialising it again changes the bytes and the check fails. Refuse a timestamp more than five minutes from your clock, so an old message replayed later is refused too.

No dependency; Node 18 or newer. import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto'; const TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 300; /** True when a CallVault webhook is genuine. `rawBody` is the request body as a Buffer. */ export function verifyCallVault(secret, headers, rawBody, now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)) { const id = headers['webhook-id']; const timestamp = headers['webhook-timestamp']; const signatures = headers['webhook-signature']; if (!id || !timestamp || !signatures || !/^\d+$/.test(timestamp)) return false; if (Math.abs(now - Number(timestamp)) > TOLERANCE_SECONDS) return false; const key = Buffer.from(secret.replace(/^whsec_/, ''), 'base64'); const expected = createHmac('sha256', key).update(`${id}.${timestamp}.`).update(rawBody).digest(); return signatures.split(' ').some((part) => { const [version, value] = part.split(','); if (version !== 'v1' || !value) return false; const given = Buffer.from(value, 'base64'); return given.length === expected.length && timingSafeEqual(given, expected); }); } With Express, read the body raw on that one route: app.post('/hooks/callvault', express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }), (req, res) => { if (!verifyCallVault(process.env.CALLVAULT_WEBHOOK_SECRET, req.headers, req.body)) { return res.sendStatus(400); } const event = JSON.parse(req.body.toString('utf8')); res.sendStatus(204); handle(event); // after answering, so slow work never runs past the 10-second wait });

Standard library only; Python 3.9 or newer. import base64 import hashlib import hmac import time TOLERANCE_SECONDS = 300 def verify_callvault(secret, headers, raw_body, now=None): """True when a CallVault webhook is genuine. raw_body is the request body as bytes.""" msg_id = headers.get("webhook-id") timestamp = headers.get("webhook-timestamp") signatures = headers.get("webhook-signature") if not msg_id or not timestamp or not signatures or not timestamp.isdigit(): return False now = int(time.time()) if now is None else now if abs(now - int(timestamp)) > TOLERANCE_SECONDS: return False key = base64.b64decode(secret.removeprefix("whsec_")) signed = f"{msg_id}.{timestamp}.".encode() + raw_body expected = base64.b64encode(hmac.new(key, signed, hashlib.sha256).digest()).decode() for part in signatures.split(" "): version, _, value = part.partition(",") if version == "v1" and hmac.compare_digest(value, expected): return True return False In Flask, pass request.headers and request.get_data(); in Django, request.headers and request.body.

Both functions above return true for this message when now is 1795269731, and false if one byte of the body changes. Use it to check your own code before pointing a real address at it. The secret is an example, not one CallVault ever issued. Value Secret whsec_dO3cgGthomKhO8+dbHiKfexif0Uh+oC6f1o5zB6hLQY= webhook-id msg_6f1c0e9a4b2d4c7e8a5f3b1d9e0c2a74 webhook-timestamp 1795269731 webhook-signature v1,KXfyLaCC7f32HlkcICIKQdzHqNy5ZrCVV+Yuevpl9DY= The body, exactly, on one line: {"type":"recording.created","timestamp":"2026-11-21T14:02:11.204Z","data":{"id":"3f6b2c1e-8d4a-4e7b-9c15-2a0d7e6f4b91","title":"Incoming call, 21 Nov, 13:49","started_at":"2026-11-21T13:49:37+00:00","duration_seconds":734,"labels":["phone_call","starred","Pixel 8"]}}

Answer with any 2xx within 10 seconds. Anything else, or no answer, is a failed try, and CallVault tries again after 5 seconds, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours, 5 hours, 10 hours and 10 hours: eight tries in all, the last about 28 hours after the first. Each try is listed under Deliveries for that address with its status and time, and Send again resends one with the same webhook-id. Two answers turn an address off: 410 Gone turns it off at once. Use it when you retire the receiver. Five days of failed deliveries turns it off, and CallVault emails you the last answer it got and how many deliveries are waiting. CallVault never follows a redirect; a 3xx counts as a failed try. After you fix the receiver, choose Turn back on.

Replace secret makes a new one. For the next 24 hours every message carries two signatures, the new secret's first, so your check passes with either. Put the new secret on your server within that day.
Pause stops sending: events that happen while it's paused aren't sent to that address later. Resume sends again from that moment. Remove address ends it for good.

Download the signed APK from the CallVault releases page, allow your browser to install apps, and open the file. CallVault isn't on Google Play. It ships as a signed APK you download from the CallVault website. You need an Android phone on 8.0 or newer. Version 1.4.0 is a prerelease for device testing; the download button on the website appears once a release is marked stable, and until then, take the APK from the releases page below. note Recording laws vary; you are responsible for getting any consent required where you are. This is general information, not legal advice.
Open the public releases page. Download the APK from the newest release. Its file name carries the build date, time and version. Download the SHA256SUMS file from the same release.

Run this where the download landed: sha256sum callvault-*.apk Compare the digest it prints against the line for your file in SHA256SUMS. They match, or you downloaded something other than the release. If they differ, don't install it. Download again.
Open the APK. Allow your browser or files app to install apps when Android asks. Confirm the install.

Open CallVault and work through Capture setup. It lists microphone, phone state and notifications under Required access, each one reading Allowed or Needs action, while the battery exemption and the optional accessibility assist sit apart from them. Allow everything that reads Needs action, then read the status line beneath them: it reads Capture is ready or Setup is incomplete. Wait for Capture is ready before you trust CallVault with anything important. Then make one real call and play it back. That test is the only honest way to learn what your phone gives you.

CallVault updates itself from the website release. It checks the release policy, downloads the APK, checks the file's size, SHA-256, version code and version name against that policy, and confirms that its package name and signing certificate match the app already installed. Only then does it open Android's installer. Nothing installs behind your back. If a check fails, the download is discarded and nothing is installed; the manual path below still works, and if neither installs, write to aoneahsan@gmail.com. Android asks once to allow CallVault to install apps, and that one permission is what the updater needs. The update screen names the version, the file and its size, with Download verified APK and View release notes. When a release becomes required, new recording pauses as soon as the phone learns of it, and the library stays readable until you install. Away from a connection nothing pauses: the phone keeps recording for 14 offline days by default (an administrator can set 1 to 365), counted from its last verified check, and past that it pauses new recording until it connects once. A server outage never uses up those days. Prefer to do it yourself? Download the newer APK from the releases page and check its SHA-256 again. Then open it exactly as you did the first time. Android replaces an app in place only when the new APK's signing certificate matches the installed one, which is the rule the updater's own signer check mirrors.
Read Permissions and onboarding, which covers what each item on Capture setup asks for.

:::warning This page is informational, not legal advice. CallVault records your own calls for personal record-keeping. Whether — and how — you may record, keep, or share a call depends on your jurisdiction and on whether you are a participant in the conversation. If you plan to do anything beyond keeping a call for your own reference, confirm the current local rules first, or consult someone who can. :::

It depends on jurisdiction, not on the phone. Many places let a participant record a conversation they are part of ("one-party consent"). Others require informing or getting consent from every party — especially before sharing or using a recording. Recording ≠ sharing. Keeping a personal record of a call you were on is generally different from publishing it, submitting it as evidence, or otherwise using it. The bar is usually higher for those. Pakistan specifically. Rules around interception and around publishing or using recordings can be involved, and differ from simply keeping a personal record of calls you took part in. Check before you use a recording beyond your own reference.

CallVault is transparent: it shows a live banner while recording and keeps a persistent notification. CallVault does not play an audible "this call is being recorded" announcement. That is a product fact — the responsibility to inform the other party where your local law requires it is yours. The developer is not a lawyer and this is not legal advice.

documents.t: CallVault asks for the smallest set of permissions it can. Capture setup shows the five that need a decision from you, each with its current state; the full list the app declares is further down this page.

Open it on first run, and again any time a call goes missing. It lists three rows under Required access, which are the microphone, the phone state and notifications, each reading Allowed or Needs action. Below them sit two rows that are not required: the battery exemption, reading Allowed or Allow, and the optional accessibility assist, reading Allowed or Open accessibility settings. Beneath the rows is the status line that decides everything: Capture is ready, or Setup is incomplete. Read that line, not the rows. "Capture is ready" means the three required rows are allowed. It does not mean every row on the screen reads Allowed, and it never will if you skip the optional ones on purpose.

Three of these are the Required access rows on Capture setup, and two more (the battery exemption and the accessibility assist) are its optional rows. The rest are declared by the app and granted by Android without asking you anything. Permission Status Why Microphone Required Record audio while a call is running Phone state Required Know when a call starts and when it ends Notifications Required Show the notification the recording service must display Foreground service (microphone) Declared Keep recording while you're in another app. Android grants this to the recording service; there is no prompt to answer Run at startup Recommended Remind you to re-arm recording after a restart Ignore battery optimizations Requested Stop the system killing the recorder in the background Modify audio settings Used Turn the speaker on when you enabled that option Install packages Used Open Android's installer for a verified update Biometric Optional The app lock Wake lock Used Keep the upload worker running Internet and network state Used Backup and update checks Storage write, Android 9 and older Used Export to Downloads

This one is off unless you turn it on in Android's accessibility settings, and it is worth knowing exactly what it is. It is a declared Android accessibility service called Call monitoring aid. It receives window-state change events. Nothing else. It can't retrieve window content, read what's on your screen, perform gestures, or reach call audio the platform doesn't hand out. It exists so CallVault stays available for call-state signals. That is all it does.

Some manufacturers stop background services hard enough to lose a recording. Allow the battery exemption when Capture setup offers it, leave the recording notification on, and if the phone still restricts CallVault, allow it in Android's own app settings too.

documents.t: The app checks for a new version, verifies the download's SHA-256 and signing certificate, and opens the Android installer for you, so an update never arrives without you confirming it. Android asks once to allow CallVault to install apps. You can also take a newer APK from the releases page and open it yourself.

Something you expected isn't there: a recording, the other person's voice, a backup, or the web library's list. Find the symptom below; each section says what causes it and what to do. note Recording laws vary; you are responsible for getting any consent required where you are. This is general information, not legal advice.

Open Capture setup. Each item under Required access reads Allowed or Needs action; the battery exemption and the optional accessibility assist sit apart from them. The status line beneath them reads Capture is ready or Setup is incomplete. Allow whatever needs action, then make a test call. Two other causes are ordinary Android behavior: After a restart or a force-stop, Android won't let an app start microphone capture in the background. CallVault posts a notification asking you to open it, and opening it re-arms capture. A required update pauses new recording until you install it; so does being away from a connection past the offline grace, until the phone connects once. The library stays readable either way.
documents.s: Why are some calls not recorded?

documents.t: Your phone decides how much of the other side a normal app can hear. An ordinary Android app can't read the phone network's call audio, so CallVault records through the microphone path and your own side is the reliable part. Turn on the speaker option. On many phones it's the only way the other person comes through clearly. Import from your phone maker's recorder if it does better. A stereo file is split into its real channels. Read the track labels before you judge the result. CallVault names only the source it actually found.

documents.t: Private cloud backup is off until you turn it on: the switch is under Settings → Storage & sync on the phone and under Profile in the web library. Sign in with Google. Backup needs an account. Uploads wait for Wi-Fi by default. Allow mobile data in the same settings if you don't want them to wait. You may be at your plan's limit, where new backups pause; nothing stored is deleted. A larger plan, or an administrator's raise, lifts the limit. Open Settings → Storage & sync → Backup & sync health for the queue, the failures and the Needs attention list.

It is probably over the 100 MB per-recording limit. A recording that size stays on the phone, is not uploaded and appears under Needs attention in Backup & sync health. Play it, export it or delete it as usual. The limit applies on every plan.

Google is the only sign-in method and it needs a working connection. Recording, playback, search, notes and export all work signed out, so a failed sign-in costs you the backup and the web library, and nothing else. The one exception is the guest limit: new recording pauses at 100, and signing in starts it again. Connect to a network and try again.

The web library shows only backed-up recordings. Turn the switch on, let an upload finish, or sign in with the phone's account; until then the list stays empty while the phone is full. Still stuck? Write to aoneahsan@gmail.com with your phone model and Android version.

Delete a recording from its detail screen, or start account deletion from Profile. For a backed-up recording, CallVault waits for server confirmation before removing any local copy; an account request also remains open if an upload's outcome needs administrator review. Read the steps below.

From a recording's detail screen you choose the scope: Delete on this phone only: removes the local file and its row from this phone, and leaves the backed-up copy where it is. Delete everywhere: asks the server to remove known cloud files and the call's details. For a signed-in recording, the app keeps any local copy and deletion state while the server checks related objects and unfinished uploads; the app removes any local copy only after the server confirms removal. If it says "Still processing on the server", retry from that recording's detail screen. For another error that persists, email aoneahsan@gmail.com. The web library can request Delete everywhere from a recording's detail view too. If CallVault shows more available cloud space while deletion is still running, that number does not confirm that every related file is gone. Retry until the server confirms removal.

Open Profile in the app or the web library, choose Delete account, and type DELETE. You can start the request yourself. If an upload's outcome is unclear, an administrator may need to check whether a private file exists and reconcile that attempt before the account request can finish. Account deletion starts removing known cloud recordings and their details. The server records unfinished upload attempts. It works through them before removing your sign-in identity. When the server cannot confirm whether an upload created a private file, an administrator must check what happened to that file before the account request can finish. No email is sent to confirm a deletion you started in the app.

Profile shows a processing state while the app asks the server to remove backed-up files. It then shows success or an error message. If it says "Still processing on the server", reopen Delete account from Profile to resume the saved request. For a different error, or if retries still cannot finish, email aoneahsan@gmail.com from your account address with the subject "Delete my CallVault data" so an administrator can check what happened. An empty file listing is not a completion signal when an upload is unresolved. Local files already on a phone are removed by the app on that phone. A copy you exported or saved to Downloads lives outside CallVault and is untouched by account deletion, so remove those yourself if you want them gone as well. :::warning This is permanent Account deletion can't be undone. If you only want to stop backing up, turn Private cloud backup off instead. That keeps every recording on the phone. :::
If you only wanted to store less, Private cloud backup covers the switch and what your plan allows.

documents.t: Sign in on the CallVault website. Choose Pro or Family and select a month or year. For Family, create a household you own and choose 3 to 5 seats. Submit the request. Each member then gets the Family limits, including 30 GB of cloud backup. Each signs in with their own Google account, the only sign-in method.

documents.t: Profile has your invite link. When 3 people you invite sign in with Google, you get 1 month of Pro, up to 6 months a year. CallVault's team can change these numbers, and Profile always shows the current ones. You see how many people joined, never who they are.

Leave or be removed, and the membership goes at once. You return to your own plan or to Free immediately: nothing stored is deleted, and new backups pause at the lower limit. The household keeps its plan until its end date, even below 3 members. The owner can't leave. The owner can delete the household instead, which removes every membership and leaves every recording where it is. Your plan and its end date are in Profile. What each limit means day to day is in private cloud backup.
Tap any recording in the list to open its detail screen, where you can listen, adjust the pace, and manage the file.

The detail screen has an audio player with the usual play/pause and a seek bar. On the phone it plays the local file; in the web app it streams the backed-up copy from its URL. Direction (incoming/outgoing), number or contact, date, duration, and your note are all shown alongside.
Use the playback-speed control to slow a call down to catch a detail or speed it up to review a long call quickly. The setting applies to the current playback session.

From the detail screen you can: Share the audio to another app. Save to Downloads to keep a copy outside CallVault. Bulk-select several recordings in the list to export or delete them together. Sharing and saving copy the audio out of CallVault's private storage — treat the exported file the way you'd treat any sensitive recording, and keep in mind the call-recording-law notes if you plan to send it on.
Deleting is covered on its own — you can remove a recording from just this device or from everywhere. See Account deletion.

Profile is the same screen on the phone (Settings → Profile) and in the web library (the Profile tab). It carries your account, your plan and its end date, your household, and the way to delete everything. The Private cloud backup switch is on Profile in the web library; on the phone it lives under Settings → Storage & sync.

Your email and the date you joined. Your display name, which you can edit. Your role and your account status are an administrator's to change rather than yours, and Roles & access covers how that grant is given, what it lets someone do, and how it is taken away again.

Profile shows the plan your account is on, with the date that plan ends. Nothing renews on its own. A plan runs to its end date and stops unless you pay for another period, and paying happens on the website rather than inside the app. A renewal extends the end date and never shortens it, so paying early costs you nothing. A plan ending deletes nothing. New backups pause at the lower limit. Nothing already stored is deleted, and every recording on the phone is untouched. Plans and Family has the limits and the prices. If you belong to a household, Profile is also where you leave it. Leaving takes effect at once and you go back to your own plan, or to Free; nothing stored is deleted, and new backups pause at the lower limit. The owner of a household can't leave it. The owner can close the household instead, which ends every membership and leaves everybody's recordings alone, though it does not end the owner's own plan, which runs to its end date.

documents.t: It is off until you turn it on. Turn it on and audio uploads as private files only you and a CallVault administrator can reach, on Wi-Fi by default. Private cloud backup is that switch's home and covers what your plan allows.

The palette icon in every header opens one panel: theme, colour, text size, corners, spacing, font, background and motion. Your choice is kept on this device and, when you're signed in, on your account, so a second device opens looking the same. CallVault ships in English and Urdu (اردو). Urdu renders right-to-left and the whole interface mirrors with it, web library included. The app follows your phone or browser locale, and you can set it explicitly here.
Deleting recordings and your account is the other thing Profile does, and it's the one worth reading before you press it.

CallVault records through the phone's microphone path, and it can import recordings another recorder already made. The list, the search, the notes and the backup are the same either way. Only how the audio reached the phone differs. note Recording laws vary; you are responsible for getting any consent required where you are. This is general information, not legal advice.

An ordinary Android app can't read the phone network's call audio, whatever any app promises. CallVault records through the phone's microphone path instead, so your own side is the reliable part, and the other person is only as clear as the phone's speaker makes them. An optional setting turns the speaker on when a call starts. Results depend on the phone.

This is the default and needs nothing unusual from the phone. A call starts, CallVault records, and the recording ends when the call does. A banner shows inside the app and a persistent notification stays visible throughout. CallVault does not announce the recording to the other person. Two things interrupt it, both Android's rule rather than a bug. After a restart or a force-stop, Android won't let an app start microphone capture in the background, so CallVault notifies you to open it again. And a recording that comes back looking silent is flagged, not filed quietly.

Nothing on this page tells you what your phone will do. One real call does. Record one and play it back. If both sides are clear enough, the microphone path is your path and you are done. If the other person is faint, turn the speaker option on and try again. Still faint, and your phone maker ships its own recorder? That recorder may reach audio an ordinary app cannot, because the phone maker wrote it and is allowed to, and the next section is for you.
documents.s: Make one test call, then decide

documents.t: If your phone maker's own recorder does better, or you run a BCR-compatible one, point CallVault at the folder that recorder writes to. CallVault imports each new file it finds there. It reads those files. It never modifies or replaces your recorder. A stereo import splits into its real channels. An import can also carry a contact name, when the recorder that made it saved one. That is the only way a name reaches CallVault, which never reads your address book and never asks to.

Every track carries the source CallVault actually found. A track is never labeled "caller" or "other party" unless that is verified, which is why some tracks read as a channel and not as a person. Where a call has at least two audible tracks whose files are still on the phone, you can ask for a combined recording: one playable mix, made on request. A one-track call has none, and nothing on the screen pretends otherwise. Read the labels before you judge the result.

Alongside the audio, CallVault stores the call's details: the number, the direction, when it started, how long it ran, which SIM handled it, the audio format and the file size. Data layer has the full list. Nothing else is kept. A recording then enters the sync pipeline, but only if you signed in and turned private cloud backup on.

documents.t: Heard what you needed? Playback and export covers the tracks and the combined mix. Heard a problem? Troubleshooting starts with the faint-other-side case.
CallVault groups recordings by day and gives you a few ways to find and organise them, on both the phone and the web app.
Search by number, contact name, or note. On the phone there's a dedicated Search tab; in the web app the search box lives at the top of the list. Your recent searches are remembered.

Narrow the list — for example to a direction or to favorites — from the filter control. In the web app the active filter and search term are kept in the URL (?filter= and ?q=), so a refresh or a shared link restores exactly what you were looking at.

Favorite a call to keep it easy to find. Add a note to a recording from its detail screen — useful for what the call was about or a follow-up. Both the favorite flag and the note sync across your devices when you're signed in, using last-write-wins: the most recent change on any device is the one that sticks.

Private cloud backup is off until you turn it on. Until then, every recording stays on this phone and nothing about a call leaves it. Turn it on and a copy reaches the web library. note Recording laws vary; you are responsible for getting any consent required where you are. This is general information, not legal advice.

Sign in with Google. It's the only sign-in method. On the phone, open Settings → Storage & sync. In the web library, open Profile. Turn on Private cloud backup. Uploads run on Wi-Fi by default. A setting in the same place allows mobile data when you'd rather not wait for Wi-Fi.

Nothing, unless you sign in and turn on private cloud backup. Then the audio uploads as private files: you can reach them in the app and in the web library, and a CallVault administrator can reach them as well. There are no public links to a recording. The web library shows only backed-up recordings, so anything you never backed up isn't there.
Every plan caps a recording at 100 MB. A longer call stays on the phone under Needs attention. Only the cloud copy is skipped. Export it to keep a copy elsewhere.

Free includes 2 GB of cloud backup, Pro 20 GB and Family 30 GB for each member; each plan also sets how many uploads an hour it accepts: 60 on Free, 300 on Pro, 600 on Family. Those are rows an administrator maintains rather than constants in the app, and an administrator can raise a limit for a single account. Plans and Family has the prices and how a paid plan reaches your account.

New backups pause. Nothing already stored is deleted, and the recordings on your phone are untouched. To back up more, move to a larger plan, ask an administrator to raise your limit, or delete recordings everywhere to free the space. When a paid plan ends, the same holds at the lower limit.

Open Settings → Storage & sync → Backup & sync health. It sits beside the Private cloud backup switch. The screen shows the queue, the retries, a row for each phone you use, and a Needs attention list for anything that stopped, each entry carrying the reason. Read that reason before you retry.

Play what you backed up from any browser. The web library shows only backed-up recordings, so a phone full of calls can sit beside an empty list. It's a view of your cloud copy rather than a second recorder, and it keeps no library of its own.
Open callvault.aoneahsan.com. Choose Sign in with Google. It's the only sign-in method. Use the same account the phone uses.

Play any recording you backed up. Read Stats: total recordings, how many are backed up, total talk time, incoming versus outgoing counts, and a bar chart of recordings per day for the last 14 days. Open Profile for the Private cloud backup switch, your preferences and the current plan with its end date. Delete a recording everywhere from its detail view. Delete your account and its cloud files. Open Security for two-step sign-in, and Other apps for access keys, assistants and webhooks. On a wide screen both sit in the side rail; on a narrow one they are rows on the Profile tab.

Private cloud backup is off until you turn it on, and one upload has to finish. Uploads run on Wi-Fi by default, and a call reaches this library only after its file has finished uploading. That switch is the first gate. Turn it on from Profile here, or from Settings → Storage & sync on the phone.

Anything that never left the phone. A recording ends up like that for one of three reasons: backup was off when you made it, its file hasn't finished uploading, or it is over the 100 MB per-recording limit. There is no per-recording "keep local" switch to look for.

Check the switch first. Then check the account. An empty library usually means private cloud backup has never been on, and the next most likely reason is that you signed in with a different Google account from the one on the phone.

Your update period starts on the day you paid, not the day the build went live. Each deployment serves its licence at /.well-known/callvault-white-label-license.json, so anyone can check it.

An update is a new signed APK your users' app installs itself, along with the backup and web library changes that go with it. That covers capture fixes when Android or a phone maker changes what an app may hear, fixes and features released to CallVault during your update period, and security fixes for sign-in, backup and the admin dashboard.
Six months of updates from the day you pay, with a licence and with a buyout.

Renewals come in 3, 6 and 12 months. A renewal adds its months to the later of today and your current end date, so renewing early loses nothing. The prices are on the updates page, where you can also renew with your licence key and the email the licence was issued to.
Your app keeps running on the last version it received. Nothing is switched off, and your users' recordings stay where they are.
Open the licence check page and enter a licence key or a domain. Verification is run by our licensing service.

A key starts with CALLVAULT-WL-. The answer is one of: Answer Meaning Valid The licence is active; the page shows the licensee, its domains and the update end date Waiting for setup Issued and paid; the deployment isn't finished yet Revoked The licence no longer covers any deployment Not found No CallVault licence has this key

The service reads https://<domain>/.well-known/callvault-white-label-license.json and checks the key it names. It reports whether the domain runs a licensed CallVault, serves a licence for a different domain, serves a revoked licence, or serves no licence file at all.

A white-label build checks its own licence once when it starts and again when it comes back to the front, never on a timer. If the licence is revoked or doesn't cover the build's domain, the app shows "This licence is not active" with a link to this check. Nothing on the phone is deleted, and an offline phone keeps working.
